title: Leadership, Identity, and Community Development
subtitle: Know what you stand for, lead groups fairly and confidently, and deliver a small, real project that improves your community.
description: A practical course for women who already lead in homes, groups and neighbourhoods, often without the title. You will clarify your identity and values, take a skills baseline, learn to run meetings and inclusive decisions, track your growth, and plan and document a costed community project with real stakeholders.
outcomes: Name your top three values as behaviours and tell a three-sentence story of self
Rate your leadership skills against a baseline and track growth with a weekly log
Run a meeting that confirms quorum, reaches a fair decision and records clear actions
Lead inclusively and safely, including handling group money with receipts and two signatories
Plan a small, fully costed community project using asset mapping, a problem tree and a SMART goal
Engage stakeholders with a power and interest grid and a specific request letter
audience: Women in Nigeria and across Africa who want to lead more confidently in their household, groups, community or civic life, whatever their level of schooling.
tools: A notebook and pen or a phone notes app
A phone camera for evidence photos (with consent)

modules.title: Who You Are and How You Already Lead
modules.overview: Leadership starts long before a title. In this module you will see leadership as influence you already use, put your identity and values into words, and take an honest baseline of your skills, blind spots, barriers and support so you know exactly where to start.

lessons.title: Leadership as influence: from the household to public life
objectives: Explain the difference between leadership as a position and leadership as influence
Name the four spheres where women lead, from household to civic life
Identify the five practices leaders carry out in any group
Recognise leadership you already practise but have not called by that name

blocks.text: Ask ten people to describe a leader and most will describe a person with a title: a chairman, a pastor, a governor, a manager. Titles matter, but they are not the whole story. In this course, **leadership means influencing people to work together toward a shared goal**. A title can give you authority, but influence comes from what you do: how you organise, decide, listen and keep your word.

This matters because many women already lead without being called leaders. The woman who keeps the records of an ajo or esusu savings group, the one who settles quarrels in the compound, the one the market women send to speak to the local government officer: each of them is influencing people toward a goal. Naming this is the first step to doing it on purpose and doing it better.
Three ideas people often mix up

head: Idea
What it means
What it looks like
rows: Position
A formal role given by election, appointment or inheritance
Treasurer of the women's fellowship, CDA secretary, ward councillor
Influence
People choose to follow your lead because they trust you
Neighbours ask your advice before deciding where to send children to school
Service
Using your role or influence for the good of the group, not only yourself
Publishing the group's accounts every month so everyone can see where money went

blocks.text: The strongest leaders combine all three: they hold a position when it is useful, they earn influence through consistent behaviour, and they use both to serve. A person with a position but no influence is obeyed only when watched. A person with influence but no sense of service can lead people in the wrong direction.
The four spheres where women lead

blocks.title: Spheres of leadership
items: Civic and public life
Community and estate
Groups and associations
Household and family
blocks.caption: Most women build leadership habits in the wider base spheres first, then carry them upward into community and civic roles.

items: **Household and family:** budgeting, planning children's education, deciding how to care for an elderly parent, resolving conflict between relatives.
**Groups and associations:** savings groups, cooperative societies, religious women's groups, market associations, alumni and town unions.
**Community and estate:** the Community Development Association (CDA), landlord and tenant associations, sanitation days, security arrangements, school parent-teacher associations.
**Civic and public life:** ward and local government meetings, elections, public hearings, advocacy to officials, boards of NGOs.

blocks.text: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 5 includes target 5.5: "Ensure women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making in political, economic and public life." This course is built around that target. It is also realistic: target 5.4 of the same goal recognises the heavy load of unpaid care and domestic work, which is one reason women's time for leadership is limited. We will plan around that, not ignore it.
Five things leaders actually do

items: **Set direction:** help the group agree what it is trying to achieve.
**Organise:** turn the goal into tasks, people and resources (money, time, tools).
**Decide:** make or guide decisions, especially when people disagree.
**Communicate:** keep everyone informed, listen, and explain the reasons behind decisions.
**Follow through:** keep promises, check progress and take responsibility when things go wrong.

blocks.title: Worked example: spotting leadership you already practise
blocks.context: Ngozi, for example, sells foodstuff in a market in Onitsha. She has run a 10-member ajo savings group for two years. Each member contributes ₦5,000 every week and one member collects the whole pot in turn.
steps: She works out the pot: 10 members × ₦5,000 = ₦50,000 collected each week, so one full cycle takes 10 weeks and every member receives ₦50,000 once.
She lists what she actually does each week: collects contributions, writes them in a notebook, reminds late payers on WhatsApp, and pays out the pot.
When two members argued about who should collect first, she suggested drawing lots in front of everyone and the group agreed.

She matches her tasks to the five practices: direction (the group's savings purpose), organising (collection and records), deciding (drawing lots), communicating (reminders), follow-through (paying out on time for two years).
blocks.result: Ngozi practises all five leadership behaviours every week. She is not starting from zero: she is starting from experience she had never named. Her next step is to use the same habits in a wider sphere, such as her market association.

blocks.title: Leadership is not dominance
blocks.text: Talking loudest, controlling money or making every decision alone is not strong leadership. It usually produces silent resentment and weak follow-through. Influence that lasts comes from fairness, clear communication and keeping your word.

blocks.name: happy-women-day
blocks.alt: A group of women standing together and celebrating
blocks.caption: Leadership in this course is something women practise together in households, groups and communities, not only on a podium.

blocks.text: Over the next eight lessons you will move from understanding to action: first you will clarify your identity, values and starting point, then practise the tools of group leadership, and finally plan and carry out a small, real contribution to your community, with evidence you can show.

takeaways: Leadership is influencing people toward a shared goal; a title is optional.
Women lead in four spheres: household, groups, community and civic life.
Every leader sets direction, organises, decides, communicates and follows through.
SDG target 5.5 calls for women's equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making.

activity.title: Map the leadership you already do
steps: Draw four boxes on a page and label them household, groups, community and civic.
In each box write any role or task you have carried out in the last 12 months.
Next to each task, write which of the five practices it shows (direction, organise, decide, communicate, follow through).
Circle the sphere where you feel most confident and underline the one you would like to grow into.
activity.evidence: A photo of your four-box leadership map with the practices labelled.

lessons.title: Identity and values: knowing what you stand for
objectives: Draw an identity map showing your roles, groups, values and story
Narrow a long list of values to your top three and define each as a behaviour
Explain how imposed "single stories" can limit how women see themselves
Write a three-sentence story of self you can use when introducing yourself as a leader

blocks.text: Your **identity** is the set of answers to the question "Who am I?" It includes the roles you hold (mother, trader, nurse, daughter-in-law), the groups you belong to (your ethnic group, faith community, town union, profession), the values you try to live by, and the story you tell about your life. Most women hold many identities at once. That is not confusion; it is a resource. Each identity connects you to different people and gives you different knowledge.

Identity matters for leadership because people follow those they understand and trust. When you know what you stand for, your decisions become more consistent, and consistency is what turns a single good act into a reputation.
Your identity map

items: **Roles:** what you do for others at home, at work and in the community.
**Groups:** the communities you belong to by birth, faith, work or choice.
**Values:** the principles that guide your choices when no one is checking.
**Story:** the key experiences that shaped you, including hardships you came through.

blocks.title: From values to influence
items: Know your values
Choose by them
Act consistently
Earn trust
Gain influence
blocks.caption: Values only build influence when they show up repeatedly in your choices, so people learn they can rely on you.

blocks.text: Finding your top three values

items: Write down 15 values that feel important, for example honesty, fairness, faith, family, hard work, independence, generosity, respect, courage, learning, excellence, peace, justice, loyalty, service.
Cross out until only 5 remain. Ask: if I had to give this one up to keep the others, could I?
Cross out two more so you have your top 3.
For each value, finish the sentence "I show this when I..." with something you actually do, not something you wish you did.
Test them: recall a hard decision from the past year. Did these values guide you? If a different value really decided it, consider swapping it in.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning values into behaviours
blocks.context: Amaka, for example, is a nurse in Enugu who also leads the welfare committee of her church women's group. She does the values sort one evening after work.
steps: She starts with 15 values and narrows to 5: honesty, fairness, family, faith and service.
She narrows to 3: honesty, fairness and service.

She writes behaviours: honesty, "I show this when I read out the welfare fund balance at every meeting"; fairness, "I show this when I use the same rule for every member who asks for support"; service, "I show this when I visit sick members myself, not only send messages".
She tests them: last month a member offered her ₦20,000 to approve her request ahead of two older requests. Amaka refused and kept the order of the list.
blocks.result: Amaka now has three values she can name and point to in action. When committee members disagree, she can explain her position by her values ("we use one rule for everyone"), which makes her decisions easier to accept.

blocks.title: When values pull in different directions
blocks.text: Values sometimes clash, for example family and service when a community task falls on your child's exam week. Decide which value leads in that specific situation, give the other a fixed time later, and tell people honestly. Clear priorities are better than half-doing both.
The danger of a single story

Other people also tell stories about who you are: "women from that area don't speak in public", "a widow should keep quiet", "she only has secondary school education". The Nigerian writer Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie describes how a single story repeated often enough becomes the only story people see. Leadership includes refusing to let one narrow story define you or the women around you.
Your story of self

The organiser and teacher Marshall Ganz uses the idea of a "story of self": a short account of why you care, rooted in a real experience, so that others understand what moves you to act. You will use yours in meetings, when asking for support and when introducing a community project. Keep it to three sentences: where you come from, a moment that made you care, and what you are doing about it now.

items: **Where I come from:** "I grew up in Aba, the eldest of five, and helped my mother sell provisions after school."
**A moment that made me care:** "When our street flooded in 2019, I watched traders lose a week of stock while everyone waited for someone else to act."
**What I am doing now:** "So I organise our monthly gutter clearing and I am learning to bring more women into our CDA's decisions."
**Check it:** is it true, short enough to say in under a minute, and does it show a value in action rather than just naming it?

blocks.title: Many identities, many bridges
blocks.text: Each identity you hold connects you to a different group. A Muslim trader who is also a member of a mixed town union can carry ideas between groups that rarely meet. Leaders who notice these bridges can bring people together who would otherwise never cooperate.

blocks.name: compass
blocks.caption: Your top three values work like a compass: they do not tell you every step, but they keep you pointed in a consistent direction.

takeaways: Identity includes your roles, groups, values and story; having many identities is a strength.
Narrow your values to three and define each as something you actually do.
Consistency between values and actions is what builds trust and influence.
Do not let a single story told about you set the limit of what you can do.

activity.title: Values sort and story of self
steps: Write 15 values on paper or in your phone notes and narrow them to 5, then to 3.
For each of the 3, write one "I show this when I..." sentence from real life.
Write a three-sentence story of self: where you come from, a moment that made you care, what you are doing now.
Read your story aloud twice, or record it as a WhatsApp voice note to yourself and listen back.
activity.evidence: Your list of three values with behaviour sentences and your written or recorded story of self.

lessons.title: Your leadership baseline: strengths, blind spots, barriers and support
objectives: Rate yourself on six core leadership skills using clear descriptions
Use the Johari window to find blind spots with help from people you trust
List the real barriers to your leadership and one practical response to each
Choose one leadership context and one skill to focus on for this course

blocks.text: A baseline is a measurement taken at the start so that you can see change later. Without one, growth is easy to forget and setbacks feel bigger than they are. In this lesson you will rate your skills, ask for outside views, name your barriers honestly and choose a single focus.
Rate six core skills
Give yourself a score from 1 (rarely) to 5 (consistently) for each skill. Score what you do now, not what you hope to do.

head: Skill
A score of 1 or 2 looks like
A score of 4 or 5 looks like
rows: Speaking up in groups
Stays silent even with a useful idea
Shares views clearly and briefly when it matters
Listening
Waits for a turn to talk, interrupts
Can repeat back others' points so they feel heard
Deciding
Delays or leaves decisions to others
Weighs options against values and decides in time
Handling disagreement
Avoids it or becomes angry
Stays calm, looks for common ground, holds firm on values
Organising people and tasks
Does everything alone or forgets tasks
Shares out tasks with names and dates
Following through
Promises often slip
Does what she says or explains early if she cannot

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a baseline
blocks.context: Halima, for example, runs a tailoring shop in Kaduna and attends her area's women's association. She completes the self-rating on her phone.
steps: Her scores: speaking up 2, listening 4, deciding 3, handling disagreement 2, organising 4, following through 5.
Total: 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 20 out of a possible 30. Average: 20 ÷ 6 = about 3.3.
Her strengths (4 and above): listening, organising and following through.
Her two lowest scores are speaking up and handling disagreement. She notices they are linked: she keeps quiet partly to avoid arguments.
She chooses one focus: speaking up in her women's association meetings.
blocks.result: Halima has a clear starting point (20 out of 30) and one specific skill to practise. In Module 2 she will track how often she speaks up and compare it with this baseline.

blocks.text: Finding blind spots: the Johari window

blocks.title: The Johari window
items: Open: known to me and others
Blind spot: others see, I don't
Hidden: I know, others don't
Unknown: no one sees yet
axes: Known to me, then not known to me
Known to others, then not known to others
blocks.caption: Feedback shrinks your blind spot and careful sharing shrinks your hidden area, so the open area where trust grows becomes larger.

blocks.text: The Johari window, created by psychologists Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham, divides what can be known about you into four areas. Your **blind spot** holds things others notice but you do not, for example that you sound impatient when tired, or that people trust you more than you think. The only way to see it is to ask. Choose two people who want good for you and ask: "What is one thing I do well when working with people, and one thing I could do better?" Write down the answers without arguing.

items: Ask by private message or face to face, not in a group chat, so people feel free to be honest.
Tell them why: "I am working on my leadership and I value your view."
Accept what they say with a simple thank you, even if it surprises you.
Look for patterns: if two people mention the same thing, treat it as a real blind spot.
Do the same exercise again at the end of the course and compare the answers.

blocks.text: Your **hidden** area also matters. Some things you keep private for good reasons, but sharing a relevant experience, for example that you once struggled to pay school fees, can make people trust your leadership on that issue. Share deliberately, not by accident.
Naming barriers honestly

items: **Time:** cooking, childcare and caring for relatives take hours each day. Response: choose roles with fixed, limited hours and negotiate shared tasks at home.
**Social expectations:** some people disapprove of women speaking in mixed meetings. Response: start where women's voices are accepted, build allies, and let results speak.
**Self-doubt:** the inner voice that says "who am I to talk?" Response: rely on your evidence (your leadership map and baseline), not your feelings alone.
**Money and transport:** meetings cost fares and data. Response: ask for meetings at accessible times and places, or join by phone or WhatsApp.
**Safety:** late evening meetings or travel alone can be risky. Response: meet in daylight, in public places, and travel with someone.

blocks.title: Pick one context and one skill
blocks.text: Trying to grow everywhere at once leads to exhaustion. Choose one context (household, a group, the community or civic life) and one skill from your baseline. You will practise it throughout Module 2.
Your support system

Leadership grows faster with three kinds of support: a **mentor** who gives advice from experience, **peers** who are growing alongside you, and a **sponsor**, a person with influence who mentions your name when opportunities come up. Write the names you already have. Empty boxes are not failure; they are a task for Module 3.

blocks.name: personal-goals
blocks.alt: A woman checking off personal goals on a board
blocks.caption: A written baseline and a single focus turn a vague wish to lead into a goal you can track.

takeaways: Rate yourself on six skills now so you can measure growth later.
Ask two trusted people for feedback to uncover your blind spots.
Name real barriers such as time, norms and safety, and plan one response to each.
Choose one context and one skill to focus on, and list your mentors, peers and sponsors.

activity.title: Build your baseline sheet
steps: Score yourself 1 to 5 on the six skills and add up your total out of 30.
Send the two Johari questions to two trusted people and write down their answers.
List your top three barriers with one practical response each.
Write your chosen context and skill, plus the names of any mentor, peer or sponsor you have.
activity.evidence: Your baseline sheet with scores, total, feedback notes, barriers and chosen focus.

quiz.q: Blessing has no title, but neighbours always ask her to help settle disputes and she organises the street's monthly sanitation. Which statement best describes her?
options: She is not a leader because she has no position
She is a leader through influence and service
She is only a helper, not a leader
She will become a leader only after an election
quiz.explain: Leadership in this course means influencing people toward a shared goal. Blessing earns influence and uses it to serve, even without a position.

quiz.q: An ajo has 12 members who each contribute ₦4,000 weekly. How much does each member receive when it is her turn?
quiz.explain: 12 members × ₦4,000 = ₦48,000 per week, which is paid to one member in turn.

quiz.q: Amaka lists "honesty" as a value. Which is the strongest way to define it for leadership?
options: "Honesty is very important to me"
"I read out the welfare fund balance at every meeting"
"Honest people are good people"
"I hope to be more honest next year"
quiz.explain: A value becomes useful for leadership when it is defined as a behaviour you actually do, which others can see and rely on.

quiz.q: In the Johari window, what is a blind spot?
options: Something you know about yourself and keep private
Something others notice about you that you do not see
Something no one knows yet
Something everyone knows, including you
quiz.explain: The blind spot holds what others see but you do not. Asking trusted people for feedback is the way to reduce it.

quiz.q: Halima scores 3, 3, 4, 2, 5 and 4 on the six baseline skills. What is her total and which skill should she consider as her focus?
options: 21; the skill scored 2
20; the skill scored 5
21; the skill scored 5
19; any skill scored 3
quiz.explain: 3 + 3 + 4 + 2 + 5 + 4 = 21 out of 30. Her lowest score (2) is the clearest place to focus her practice.

modules.title: Leadership Practice: Meetings, Inclusion and Tracking Growth
modules.overview: This module gives you the working tools of group leadership. You will learn to run a meeting that ends in a clear decision, lead in a way that includes everyone and keeps people and money safe, and keep a simple log that shows your leadership growing week by week.

lessons.title: Running a meeting that reaches a clear decision
objectives: Prepare an agenda and assign the chair, secretary and timekeeper roles
Lead a meeting through the standard order from opening to next date
Choose between consensus, majority vote, consult-then-decide and delegation
Record decisions as minutes with who does what by when

blocks.text: Much of community leadership happens in meetings: the women's association, the cooperative, the CDA, the parent-teacher association. Poorly run meetings drag on, end without a decision and leave people grumbling afterwards. Well run meetings are short, fair and end with clear actions. This is a skill you can learn step by step.
Before the meeting

items: **Purpose:** write in one sentence what the meeting must achieve, for example "agree how members will pay for the new canopy".
**Agenda:** a short numbered list of items, shared at least two days ahead on the group's WhatsApp, so people come prepared.
**Roles:** the **chair** guides discussion and keeps order; the **secretary** records decisions; the **timekeeper** watches the clock.
**Quorum:** check your group's constitution or rules for the minimum number of members needed for decisions to count.
**Time and place:** choose a time women can attend, for example after market hours, and a safe, accessible venue.

blocks.text: The order of a meeting

blocks.title: Meeting flow
items: Open and confirm quorum
Adopt last minutes
Discuss each item
Decide and record
Assign actions
Fix next date
blocks.caption: Following the same order every time makes meetings predictable, fair and much shorter.

blocks.text: Open with the customary greeting or prayer, then confirm that quorum is present. Read the minutes of the last meeting and ask a member to move that they are adopted as a true record. Review "matters arising", meaning actions from last time. Take each agenda item in turn: the chair introduces it, invites views, summarises, then moves to a decision. End with any other business, the date of the next meeting and a close.
Four ways to decide

head: Method
How it works
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Consensus
Discuss until everyone can accept the decision
Small groups, decisions that need everyone's commitment
Can take long; a few people can block
Majority vote
The option with more than half of the votes cast wins
Larger groups, clear choices
The losing side may feel left out; explain and include them
Consult then decide
Leader hears views, then decides and explains why
Urgent or technical issues
Only works if people trust the leader
Delegate
Group hands the decision to a person or committee
Detailed tasks such as choosing a supplier
Set limits, for example a maximum amount to spend

blocks.title: Worked example: deciding a levy fairly
blocks.context: A market women's association in Ibadan has 40 members. For example, its rules say quorum is half the members. The members want a new canopy. The quote is about ₦360,000 (an approximate price; get your own quotes).
steps: Agenda shared on WhatsApp three days ahead: item 2 is "How to pay for the canopy".
On the day 26 members attend. Quorum is 40 ÷ 2 = 20, and 26 is more than 20, so decisions are valid.
The treasurer presents two options. Option A: a one-off levy of ₦360,000 ÷ 40 = ₦9,000 per member. Option B: the same ₦9,000 paid as ₦3,000 per month for 3 months.
After discussion the chair calls a vote. 17 vote for B, 6 for A, 3 abstain. Votes cast: 17 + 6 = 23; more than half of 23 is 12 or more, and 17 is more than 12, so B wins.
The secretary records: decision B; treasurer to collect ₦3,000 per member monthly, issue receipts and report the balance at each meeting; canopy ordered once ₦360,000 is in the account.
blocks.result: The meeting ends with one clear decision, a fair payment plan, a named person responsible and a way for every member to check the money. Absent members can read the minutes on WhatsApp and know exactly what to pay.

blocks.title: Minutes that people actually use
blocks.text: Good minutes are short. For each item record only the decision, the person responsible and the deadline. Share them within 48 hours so memories are fresh and disagreements about what was agreed are settled quickly.
Chairing skills for difficult moments

items: **Someone dominates:** thank them, summarise their point in one sentence, then say "Let us hear from those who have not spoken yet."
**Discussion goes in circles:** summarise the options on the table and ask "Are we ready to decide, or is there new information?"
**An off-topic issue comes up:** write it down as "parked" and promise a time to discuss it, under any other business or at the next meeting.
**Tempers rise:** call a five-minute break, speak to the people involved separately, then return to the facts.

blocks.text: Start with why

People commit more readily when they understand the purpose, not only the task. Before asking a group to contribute money or time, explain why it matters to them: "We lose sales every rainy season because customers avoid our wet stalls" is more persuasive than "We need a canopy". Simon Sinek's well-known talk explains this idea of starting with why.

blocks.name: meeting
blocks.alt: People seated around a table in a meeting
blocks.caption: A clear agenda, fixed roles and recorded decisions turn a long talk into a meeting that gets things done.

takeaways: Share a short agenda ahead and assign chair, secretary and timekeeper.
Confirm quorum before making decisions that bind the group.
Pick the decision method that fits the group and the issue.
Record each decision with a person responsible and a deadline, and share minutes within 48 hours.

activity.title: Plan or observe a meeting
steps: Choose a real meeting you will attend or lead in the next two weeks.
Write a one-sentence purpose and a numbered agenda of no more than five items.
Note which decision method fits the main item and why.
After the meeting, write minutes for one item: decision, person responsible, deadline.
activity.evidence: Your agenda and one item of minutes, or a photo of them.

lessons.title: Inclusive, safe and sustainable leadership
objectives: Identify who is often left out of community decisions and why
Apply at least four techniques that bring quiet and excluded voices in
Follow basic safeguarding, money and data protection practices as a leader
Respond to public pushback calmly and turn it into a workable next step

blocks.text: A decision made by a few people for many people often fails, because those left out do not trust it, do not follow it, or were the ones who knew why it would not work. **Inclusive leadership** means everyone affected by a decision has a fair chance to be heard. It is not a favour; it produces better decisions.
Who is often left out

items: Women with disabilities, who may not reach upstairs or distant venues.
Older women and widows, whose views are sometimes dismissed.
Young women, who may be told to wait their turn.
Women who cannot read, when decisions are shared only in writing.
Newcomers or women who speak a different first language.
Women working at the meeting time, such as traders or shift workers.

blocks.text: Techniques that widen the circle

items: **Go round the room:** give every person a short turn before open discussion, so quieter members speak before the loudest set the direction.
**Small groups first:** split into groups of four or five to discuss, then each group reports back.
**Choose access:** ground-floor venues, times after market hours, and a phone or WhatsApp option for those who cannot travel.
**Use shared languages:** allow contributions in Pidgin, Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba or another local language and arrange someone to interpret.
**Read decisions aloud:** never rely only on written notices.
**Collect private input:** a suggestion box or private WhatsApp messages for people who will not speak in public.

blocks.title: Inclusion check before any meeting
items: Suitable time and place
Accessible venue
Language everyone understands
Every voice invited
Decisions read back aloud
blocks.caption: Running through this short checklist before each meeting catches most of the reasons people end up excluded.

blocks.text: Keeping people, money and information safe

Leaders carry a duty of care. **Safeguarding** means protecting people, especially children and vulnerable adults, from harm during activities you organise. Practical habits: never leave a child alone with one adult behind a closed door during group activities; ask permission before taking or posting anyone's photo, and a parent's permission for children; and know where to refer someone who discloses abuse, such as a trusted health facility, the police or a recognised support organisation in your state.

blocks.title: Group money and personal data
blocks.text: Use a group bank account with at least two signatories, issue receipts for every payment, and report balances at every meeting. Never share members' phone numbers, addresses or ID details outside the group without their consent: Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for handling personal data. Beware of scams that ask leaders to pay a fee to receive a grant; genuine funders do not charge to release money.
When someone pushes back in public

blocks.title: Worked example: turning pushback into a trial
blocks.context: Fatima, for example, lives in an estate in Kano. At a CDA meeting she proposes that women have a seat on the executive committee. An elder objects loudly that this is not how things have been done.
steps: She lets him finish without interrupting, then summarises his point: "You are concerned that changing the committee could cause division."
She connects to a shared goal: "We all want the estate safe and clean, and women run most of the sanitation work."
She proposes a small, time-limited step: one women's representative, attending executive meetings for 6 months, then a review.
Before the next meeting she visits two respected members privately to explain the proposal and ask for support.
At the next meeting the trial is approved by vote, with the review date written in the minutes.
blocks.result: Instead of a public fight, Fatima secured a concrete trial with a review date. The elder's concern was heard, and the women gained a real voice that can be judged on results.

blocks.text: Pushback is common when women step into visible roles. Treat it as information: what is the person actually worried about? Respond to the worry, keep your tone calm, and offer a small, reversible step. Allies who speak for you are often more persuasive than speaking for yourself. If pushback turns into threats or harassment, put your safety first, document what happened and seek help from trusted leaders.
Leading without burning out

A leader who takes every task ends up exhausted and leaves the group dependent on her. Limit yourself to one or two roles at a time, share tasks with named people and dates, and rest without guilt. Training someone else to do part of your job is itself an act of leadership.

When you delegate, be specific: name the task, the person, the deadline, the resources available and how they should report back. "Kemi, please collect quotes for chairs from three shops by Friday and post them on the group" works far better than "someone should look into chairs". Check in once halfway, then let the person do it their way.

blocks.name: together
blocks.alt: A small group of people standing together
blocks.caption: Inclusive leadership brings everyone affected into the circle, which makes decisions stronger and easier to carry out.

takeaways: Inclusive decisions are better decisions because more knowledge and trust go into them.
Go-round turns, small groups, accessible venues and shared languages bring excluded voices in.
Protect people, money and data: safeguarding, two signatories and receipts, consent before sharing.
Answer pushback by naming the worry, linking to a shared goal and offering a small trial.

activity.title: Inclusion audit of one group
steps: Pick one group you belong to and list who usually speaks and who rarely does.
Run the five-point inclusion checklist on its last meeting and note any gaps.
Choose one technique to suggest or use at the next meeting.
Check how the group handles money: are there two signatories and receipts? Note what is missing.
activity.evidence: Your completed checklist with one inclusion technique and one money-safety improvement written down.

lessons.title: Tracking your leadership growth with a log and feedback
objectives: Keep a weekly leadership log that records situations, actions and results
Compare your log against your Module 1 baseline using simple counts
Request and record feedback using Stop, Start, Continue
Distinguish outputs from outcomes when measuring community contributions

blocks.text: Leadership growth can feel invisible because it happens in small moments. A log makes it visible. Five minutes a week is enough to record what you did, how it went and what you will try next. Over a month the pattern becomes clear, and that evidence feeds your capstone portfolio.
The leadership log

head: Date
Situation
Skill
What I did
Result
Next time
rows: 3 Mar
Women's association meeting on dues
Speaking up
Suggested monthly instead of yearly dues
Adopted after discussion
Prepare my point in writing first
10 Mar
Disagreement with sister-in-law over school fees
Handling disagreement
Listened fully, then stated my view once
Calmer talk, no decision yet
Agree a date to decide

blocks.text: Write in your notebook or a phone notes app. Keep it honest: record the times you stayed silent too, with what stopped you. Those entries are just as useful because they show you what to practise.

items: **Situation:** where it happened and who was there, in a few words.
**Skill:** the one skill from your baseline that the moment called for.
**What I did:** your actual words or actions, not your intentions.
**Result:** what happened next, including how people responded.
**Next time:** one small change you will try, so every entry ends with a lesson.

blocks.title: Make logging a habit
blocks.text: Attach logging to something you already do weekly, such as Sunday evening or the day you restock your shop. A WhatsApp chat with only yourself, or a voice note, works well if writing is slow for you.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing four weeks against a baseline
blocks.context: Halima, for example, chose speaking up as her focus with a baseline score of 2. She counts every time she shared a view in a group setting.
steps: Week 1: 1 time. Week 2: 2 times. Week 3: 2 times. Week 4: 4 times.
Total: 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9 times in four weeks. Average: 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 times a week.
From week 1 to week 4 the count went from 1 to 4, four times as often.
Two of her suggestions were adopted by the group and one was rejected; she notes what made the adopted ones work (she prepared them in writing first).
She re-rates speaking up at the end of week 4: 3 out of 5, up from 2.
blocks.result: Halima has clear evidence of growth: a rising count, two adopted suggestions and a one-point rise on her self-rating. She keeps the same focus for another month and aims for at least 3 times a week.

blocks.text: Getting feedback: Stop, Start, Continue

items: Choose one or two people who saw you in action, such as a fellow group member.
Ask three short questions: what should I stop doing, start doing and continue doing when I lead?
Listen and write the answers without defending yourself; say thank you.
Pick one point to act on and record it in your log.

blocks.text: Measuring what you do for the community

blocks.title: Outputs and outcomes
items: Outputs: what we did
Outcomes: what changed
right: Street no longer floods after rain
blocks.caption: Outputs show effort; outcomes show whether life actually improved, so track both.

blocks.text: **Outputs** are the activities you carried out and are easy to count. **Outcomes** are the changes that result, and they take longer. A good tracker records both: "We held three clearing days (output) and the street did not flood in the next two heavy rains (outcome)." You will use this when planning your community project in Module 3.
Choosing simple indicators

An **indicator** is a sign you can count or observe that tells you whether things are changing. Good indicators are few, easy to collect and linked to your goal. For personal growth, count the behaviour you are practising. For a community activity, pick one output and one outcome indicator and note them on the same day each month.

head: Goal
Output indicator
Outcome indicator
How to collect
rows: Speak up more in meetings
Number of times I shared a view
Number of my suggestions adopted
Leadership log after each meeting
Bring more women into CDA meetings
Number of invitations sent
Number of women attending
Attendance list at each meeting
Keep the street from flooding
Number of clearing days held
Number of heavy rains without flooding
Notes and photos after rain

blocks.title: Never inflate your numbers
blocks.text: Report what really happened, including small numbers and failures. Exaggerated results destroy trust when people check, and funders and officials often do. An honest "12 people came, fewer than we hoped" is far stronger than a doubtful "over 100 people".
Set a monthly review: read your log, total your counts, re-rate your focus skill out of 5, and decide whether to keep the same focus or move to the next lowest skill on your baseline.

blocks.name: progress-tracking
blocks.caption: A weekly log and monthly review turn small leadership moments into clear evidence of growth.

takeaways: A five-minute weekly log makes leadership growth visible.
Compare simple counts and re-ratings with your baseline every month.
Stop, Start, Continue is a quick, safe way to ask for feedback.
Track both outputs (what you did) and outcomes (what changed), honestly.

activity.title: Start your leadership log
steps: Set up a log with the six columns: date, situation, skill, what I did, result, next time.
Record at least three entries over the next two weeks, including one time you held back.
Ask one person the Stop, Start, Continue questions and write the answers.
At the end of two weeks count your entries and re-rate your focus skill out of 5.
activity.evidence: Your log with at least three entries, feedback notes and your new rating.

quiz.q: A cooperative has 30 members and its rules set quorum at half the members. 14 members arrive. What should the chair do?
options: Hold the vote; most of those present agree
Discuss the items but postpone binding decisions until quorum is met
Ask the 14 to vote on behalf of the absent members
Cancel the cooperative's plans
quiz.explain: Quorum is 30 ÷ 2 = 15. With 14 present, decisions would not be valid, so binding decisions should wait.

quiz.q: In a vote, 11 members choose option A, 9 choose option B and 4 abstain. Under simple majority of votes cast, what is the result?
options: No decision, because 11 is less than half of 24
Option B wins
Option A wins, because 11 is more than half of the 20 votes cast
The chair must decide
quiz.explain: Votes cast are 11 + 9 = 20. More than half of 20 is 11 or more, so option A passes.

quiz.q: Which minutes entry is most useful?
options: "Long discussion about the canopy"
"Members were happy"
"Canopy to be discussed further"
"Treasurer to collect ₦3,000 per member monthly from April, report at each meeting"
quiz.explain: Good minutes record the decision, the person responsible and the deadline, so everyone knows what happens next.

quiz.q: During a meeting, the same three women do all the talking while others stay silent. What is the best next step for the chair?
options: Go round the room and give each person a short turn
End the meeting early
Ask the quiet women why they never contribute
Let the three women decide since they are most interested
quiz.explain: A go-round gives every member a turn before open discussion, so quieter voices are heard without being singled out.

quiz.q: Which of these is an outcome rather than an output?
options: Three sanitation days were held
40 flyers were shared on WhatsApp
The street did not flood after the next two heavy rains
One letter was sent to the councillor
quiz.explain: Outputs are activities carried out; an outcome is a change in conditions, such as the street no longer flooding.

quiz.q: Someone messages the women's group treasurer saying a grant of ₦2 million is approved but she must first pay a ₦50,000 processing fee. What should she do?
options: Pay quickly so the group does not lose the grant
Pay half and ask for the rest later
Treat it as a likely scam, pay nothing and verify with the funder through official contacts
Share members' bank details so the funder can pay them directly
quiz.explain: Genuine funders do not charge fees to release grants. She should pay nothing, protect members' data and verify independently.

modules.title: Community Development in Action
modules.overview: Now you put leadership to work for your community. You will find a real need and the assets already present, plan a small, affordable project, bring the right stakeholders and mentors on board, and finish with a portfolio and a 90-day plan that keeps you growing.

lessons.title: From need to action: planning a small community project
objectives: Gather information on a community need using a walk, conversations and records
Map community assets using the six categories of asset-based community development
Separate a problem's root causes from its effects with a problem tree
Write a SMART project goal with a simple, fully costed budget

blocks.text: **Community development** means people working together to improve conditions in their own community, using their own knowledge and resources first and outside help second. Your project does not need to be large. A well run small project that people can see and trust is the best foundation for bigger ones.

A useful approach is **Asset-Based Community Development (ABCD)**, associated with John McKnight and John Kretzmann. Instead of starting with a list of what the community lacks, it starts by mapping what the community already has. People who are only described by their needs tend to wait for rescue; people who see their assets start acting.
Step 1: Listen and look

items: **Community walk:** walk the area with two or three others and note problems and resources you see (blocked drains, an empty hall, a busy borehole).
**Conversations:** ask at least 10 people from different groups the same two questions: what would make life here better, and what are you willing to do about it?
**Existing information:** check notices, CDA records, the school or primary health centre, which may already know key facts.
**Community meeting:** share what you found and let people choose priorities.

blocks.text: Step 2: Map your assets

head: Asset type
Examples in a Nigerian community
rows: Individuals
A retired teacher, a woman who keeps excellent records, youths with phones and data
Associations
Women's fellowship, market association, town union, age grades, cooperatives
Institutions
Schools, primary health centre, mosque or church, local government offices
Physical assets
Community hall, open land, boreholes, roads, shops
Economic assets
Local businesses, savings groups, market days
Culture and stories
Festivals, shared history, traditions of communal work

blocks.text: Step 3: Find the root cause

A **problem tree** helps you avoid solving the wrong problem. Write the main problem in the middle (the trunk). Below it, write the causes (the roots): ask "why does this happen?" several times. Above it, write the effects (the branches): what happens because of the problem. Then choose a root cause that your group can actually act on. Fixing a root cause solves the problem for longer; treating only an effect means you will be back next season facing the same trouble.

blocks.title: Small project cycle
items: Listen and look
Map assets
Choose one root cause
Plan with SMART goal
Act together
Review and share results
blocks.caption: Each step builds on the one before, and sharing results at the end builds trust for the next project.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a drainage clearing project
blocks.context: Chioma, for example, lives on a street in Port Harcourt with 30 households. Every rainy season the street floods and some shops close. On the community walk her team finds the main gutter blocked with refuse and sand.
steps: Problem tree: problem is flooding; root causes are refuse dumped in the gutter and no regular clearing; effects are lost sales, damaged goods and stagnant water that breeds mosquitoes.
Assets: 12 residents willing to work one Saturday a month, a church compound to store tools, a resident with a pickup who will carry waste to the approved dumpsite.

Budget (approximate prices, check your own market): 3 shovels at ₦7,500 = ₦22,500; 2 rakes at ₦4,000 = ₦8,000; 20 pairs of heavy gloves at ₦1,000 = ₦20,000. Total: ₦22,500 + ₦8,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦50,500.
Contribution: ₦50,500 ÷ 30 households = about ₦1,683, rounded up to ₦1,700. Collected: 30 × ₦1,700 = ₦51,000, leaving ₦500 kept as a recorded balance.
SMART goal: "By the end of June, residents will clear the main gutter on the first Saturday of every month, so that the street does not flood after heavy rain."
blocks.result: Chioma's team has a cheap, specific project based on a root cause, funded by the community itself, with every naira accounted for. It is small enough to succeed and visible enough to build trust.

blocks.title: Working safely on clean-ups
blocks.text: Wear gloves and closed shoes or boots, never handle broken glass or sharp metal with bare hands, keep children away from the work, do not enter fast-flowing water, and wash hands with soap and clean water afterwards. Take waste to an approved dumpsite and never into a river or canal.
A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Test yours: could a neighbour tell, on a fixed date, whether it was achieved? If not, make it more specific.
Choosing a first project wisely

items: **Felt need:** many people, not only you, named it in the conversations.
**Within your control:** the group can act mostly with its own time, skills and money.
**Affordable:** the cost per household or member is small enough that most can pay.
**Visible:** people will see the result, which builds trust for the next project.
**Safe and lawful:** it needs no risky work and does not break local rules; check with the CDA or LGA if unsure.

blocks.name: idea-to-plan
blocks.alt: A person turning an idea into a written plan
blocks.caption: Moving from a felt problem to a costed, time-bound plan is the step that turns concern into community action.

takeaways: Start with what the community already has, not only what it lacks.
Use a walk, at least 10 conversations and existing records before deciding.
A problem tree helps you act on a root cause instead of a symptom.
Write a SMART goal and a fully costed budget with approximate, checked prices.

activity.title: Map and plan
steps: Do a short community walk with at least one other person and note 5 problems and 5 assets.
Ask 10 people the two listening questions and record their answers.
Draw a problem tree for the most common problem and circle one root cause you can act on.
Write a SMART goal and a simple budget with total cost and cost per household or member.
activity.evidence: Your notes, problem tree drawing, SMART goal and budget.

lessons.title: Stakeholders, partners and mentors: building support for your project
objectives: Name the local stakeholders who can help or block a community project
Place stakeholders on a power and interest grid and decide how to engage each
Write a short, specific request letter to an official or organisation
Find a mentor and peers and offer support to another woman in return

blocks.text: No community project succeeds on one person's energy. A **stakeholder** is anyone who affects or is affected by your project. Some can give permission, money or labour; some can block you if they feel ignored. Leading well means knowing who they are and talking to the right people at the right time.

Respect local protocol. In many communities, visiting the traditional or community head before a public activity is expected courtesy, and skipping it can turn a supporter into an opponent. Ask an older member how things are usually done, and go with one or two others rather than alone so the visit represents the group, not just you.
Who's who in your community

items: **Traditional and community heads:** the Baale, Obi, Emir's representative or village head, whose blessing often opens doors.
**Community Development Association (CDA) and landlords' associations:** organise residents and often run sanitation and security.
**Elected officials:** your ward councillor and the Local Government Area (LGA) chairman's office, which manage local services such as waste collection.
**Religious bodies:** churches and mosques with halls, members and trust.
**Schools and primary health centres:** institutions with staff and information.
**NGOs and community-based organisations (CBOs):** may offer training, materials or small grants.
**Women's groups and market associations:** your natural allies and labour force.

blocks.text: Mapping power and interest

blocks.title: Stakeholder power and interest grid
items: Keep satisfied
Work closely with
Monitor
Keep informed
blocks.caption: Spend most effort on high-power, high-interest stakeholders, while keeping powerful but less interested people satisfied and supporters informed.

blocks.text: The grid places each stakeholder by **power** (how much they can help or block you) and **interest** (how much they care about this project). High power and high interest: work closely, involve them in planning. High power, low interest: keep them satisfied with short, respectful updates. Low power, high interest: keep them informed; they are often your most loyal volunteers. Low power, low interest: monitor and share results publicly.

blocks.title: Worked example: placing stakeholders for the drainage project
blocks.context: Chioma's street project, for example, needs regular refuse pickup so the gutter stays clear after each clearing day.
steps: Ward councillor: high power, medium interest. Keep satisfied: send a short letter and invite her to the first clearing day.
CDA chairman: high power, high interest. Work closely: present the plan at the CDA meeting and ask for it to be adopted as a CDA activity.
Shop owners on the street: lower power, high interest. Keep informed: weekly WhatsApp update with photos and the money balance.
Residents of the next street: low power, low interest for now. Monitor: share results publicly; they may want to copy the project.
blocks.result: Chioma knows where to spend her limited time. The CDA adopts the project, the councillor attends the first clearing day and arranges a refuse pickup, and shop owners contribute water and snacks for volunteers.

blocks.text: Asking well: the request letter

items: **Who we are:** one sentence naming your group and how many households or members it represents.
**What we have already done:** show your own effort first, for example "30 households contributed ₦51,000 and cleared the gutter on 1 June".
**The specific ask:** one clear request, such as weekly refuse collection from a named point.
**Why it matters:** the outcome you expect, such as no flooding and fewer mosquitoes.
**Contact and follow-up:** a name, phone number and the date you will follow up.

blocks.title: Transparency builds partners
blocks.text: Post a simple account after every activity on your group's WhatsApp: money in, money out, balance, with photos of receipts. Officials and NGOs are far more willing to support groups that already show honest records.

Follow up on the date you promised, politely and briefly. If the answer is no, ask what would make a yes possible later, or who else could help. A refusal today often becomes support once the official sees your project working. Keep a simple record of every contact: who, when, what was asked and what was said.
The first follower

Movements often begin when one person acts and a second person publicly joins in. That first follower shows others it is safe to join. As a leader, welcome and honour your first followers by name; as a member, sometimes the bravest leadership is to be the first follower of another woman's good idea.
Mentors, peers and giving back

Approach a possible mentor with a specific request: "Could I ask you three questions about how you got the CDA to support women's projects, for 20 minutes next week?" Specific requests are easier to accept than "please mentor me". Join or form a peer circle of three to five women who meet monthly to share progress. And support another woman's growth now, even while you are still learning: reciprocity strengthens both of you.

blocks.name: handshake
blocks.caption: Partnerships with officials, associations and mentors give a small project the reach and staying power one person cannot.

takeaways: List everyone who can help or block your project before you start.
Use the power and interest grid to decide how much time each stakeholder gets.
Request letters work best when they show your own effort first and make one specific ask.
Honour first followers, find a mentor with a specific request, and support other women in turn.

activity.title: Stakeholder map and request
steps: List at least six stakeholders for your planned project.
Draw the power and interest grid and place each stakeholder in a quadrant.
Write a five-part request letter or WhatsApp message to one high-power stakeholder.
Write a specific mentoring request to one woman whose leadership you respect.
activity.evidence: Your stakeholder grid, request letter and mentoring request (sent or ready to send).

lessons.title: Your leadership and community impact portfolio and 90-day plan
objectives: Write a structured reflection using What? So what? Now what?
Assemble evidence of a real household or community leadership contribution
Build a 90-day plan with monthly milestones for leadership and community impact
Plan how to hand over or sustain your project so it does not depend only on you

blocks.text: This lesson brings everything together into your capstone, the Leadership and Community Impact Project. It has three parts: a written reflection on your values, strengths and one leadership skill practised in a real situation; documentation of a specific household or community contribution; and a 90-day plan naming your next leadership goal and community step.
Part 1: Reflection with What? So what? Now what?

This three-question model, set out by Gary Rolfe and colleagues, keeps reflection practical. **What?** describes what happened. **So what?** explains what it means and what you learned, linked to your values and strengths. **Now what?** states what you will do differently next time. Aim for 300 to 500 words, written or recorded as a voice note and transcribed. Be honest about what did not go well: a reflection that admits a mistake and shows what you learned is more convincing than one that only lists successes.

blocks.title: Worked example: a short reflection and plan
blocks.context: Halima, for example, focused on speaking up in her women's association in Kaduna and supported a market sanitation day.
steps: What? "Over four weeks I spoke up 9 times. I proposed monthly dues instead of yearly dues and the association adopted it. I also organised 15 women for a sanitation day around our market section."

So what? "My values are fairness, service and hard work. Monthly dues are fairer for traders with small daily income. I learned that preparing my point in writing first makes me calm and clear. My blind spot, from feedback, was that I give up too quickly when someone disagrees."
Now what? "I will hold my point at least once more when challenged, and ask for a vote rather than dropping the idea."
Baseline comparison: speaking up rose from 2 to 3 out of 5; total baseline score rose from 20 to 22 out of 30.
Evidence attached: log pages, the minutes showing the dues decision, a group photo taken with consent and the sanitation day attendance list.
blocks.result: Halima's reflection is specific, linked to her values and backed by evidence. Anyone reading it can see what she did, what she learned and what she will do next.

blocks.text: Part 2: Documenting your contribution

items: **Minutes or notes** showing a decision you proposed or led.
**Attendance lists** with names and phone numbers kept private.
**Receipts and accounts** for any money handled.
**Before and after photos**, taken with permission, with no children's faces posted publicly without parental consent.
**Short statements** from one or two people who took part, in their own words.

blocks.text: Part 3: Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: 90-day plan
items: Days 1 to 30: prepare
Days 31 to 60: act
Days 61 to 90: review
Day 90: share results
blocks.caption: Breaking 90 days into three monthly phases makes progress easy to check and adjust.

head: Month
Leadership goal action
Community step
Evidence
rows: Month 1
Speak up at least 3 times a week; log each
Present the project plan at the CDA meeting
Log pages, CDA minutes
Month 2
Hold my point once when challenged and ask for a vote
Run two clearing days with at least 12 volunteers
Attendance lists, photos, accounts
Month 3
Ask two people Stop, Start, Continue; re-rate all six skills
Report results and train a deputy coordinator
Feedback notes, new baseline, handover note

blocks.title: Plan for handover from the start
blocks.text: A project that collapses when you are busy was never fully a community project. From month 1, name a deputy, share the records with two people, and write a one-page note on how the project runs. Training a successor is one of the clearest signs of mature leadership.

Keep your plan realistic for your time. If caring duties are heavy this quarter, choose fewer, smaller steps and complete them. Finished small steps build more confidence and trust than ambitious plans abandoned halfway.
Sharing results with the community

Reporting back is part of leadership, not an extra. At the end of your project or at day 90, give a short report at a meeting and on WhatsApp: what you set out to do, what was done (outputs), what changed (outcomes), the money in, money out and balance, who helped, and what comes next. Thank volunteers by name, and invite questions about the accounts openly rather than waiting for complaints. Keep the report under five minutes so people actually listen. People who see their effort recognised are far more likely to join the next activity.

items: **Common mistake:** a plan with ten goals. Keep one leadership goal and one community step per month.
**Common mistake:** no evidence collected until the end. Take notes and photos as you go.
**Common mistake:** money reported only when someone asks. Report balances every time.
**Common mistake:** doing it all yourself. Name a deputy in month 1.

blocks.name: master-plan
blocks.alt: A woman pinning a plan to a board
blocks.caption: A written 90-day plan turns what you learned in this course into steps you can check off and share.

takeaways: Reflect with What? So what? Now what? and link each answer to your values.
Back every claim with evidence: minutes, receipts, attendance, consented photos.
Split your 90-day plan into monthly leadership and community steps with evidence.
Name a deputy and share records early so the project outlives your involvement.

activity.title: Assemble your capstone
steps: Write your reflection using What? So what? Now what? in 300 to 500 words.
Gather at least three pieces of evidence of your household or community contribution.
Fill in a three-month plan table with leadership actions, community steps and evidence.
Re-rate yourself on the six baseline skills and record the change from Module 1.
activity.evidence: Your reflection, evidence folder (photos or scans) and completed 90-day plan.

options: Listing everything the community lacks
Waiting for government to identify problems
Mapping the skills, groups, institutions and resources the community already has
Applying for a large grant
quiz.explain: ABCD starts from existing assets so people see what they can do themselves before seeking outside help.

quiz.q: A street of 25 households needs tools costing ₦40,000 in total. What is the contribution per household?
On a problem tree, "refuse dumped in the gutter" is best placed as:
options: An effect (branch)
A root cause
The trunk (main problem) only
An asset
quiz.explain: It explains why the flooding happens, so it is a root cause. Lost sales and stagnant water are effects.

quiz.q: The LGA waste department has high power but little interest in your street project. On the power and interest grid you should:
options: Ignore them
Work closely with them on every detail
Monitor them only
Keep them satisfied with short, respectful updates and a specific ask
quiz.explain: High power, low interest stakeholders should be kept satisfied: brief, respectful contact and clear requests.

quiz.q: Which request letter opening is strongest?
options: "Our 30 households raised ₦51,000 and cleared the gutter on 1 June; we ask for weekly refuse pickup"
"Please help our poor community with anything you can"
"We need money for many projects"
"You have neglected our street for years"
quiz.explain: It shows the community's own effort first and makes one specific request, which officials find easier to support.

quiz.q: In What? So what? Now what?, the "Now what?" part should contain:
options: A description of what happened
What you learned about your values
What you will do differently next time
A list of people who attended
quiz.explain: Now what? turns reflection into a concrete next action.

finalQuiz.q: Which definition of leadership does this course use?
options: Holding an elected or appointed title
Influencing people to work together toward a shared goal
Being the loudest voice in a meeting
Controlling a group's money
finalQuiz.explain: Leadership here is influence toward a shared goal; titles are useful but optional.

options: Ending hunger
Clean water and sanitation
Women's full participation and equal opportunities for leadership in decision-making
Free primary education
finalQuiz.explain: Target 5.5 calls for women's full and effective participation and equal opportunities for leadership at all levels of decision-making.

finalQuiz.q: Which value statement is most useful for a leader?
options: "I value fairness"
"Fairness is good"
"I want to be fairer one day"
"I show fairness when I use the same rule for every member who asks for support"
finalQuiz.explain: Defining a value as an observable behaviour makes it consistent and trustworthy.

finalQuiz.q: Ada scores 2, 3, 3, 4, 2 and 4 on the six baseline skills. What is her average score?
options: About 3.0
About 2.5
About 3.5

finalQuiz.q: Which action shrinks your Johari blind spot?
options: Keeping private matters hidden
Asking trusted people for honest feedback
Avoiding meetings
Rating yourself higher
finalQuiz.explain: The blind spot is what others see and you do not, so feedback is how you discover it.

finalQuiz.q: An association of 50 members has a quorum of half. 22 members attend. Can it make binding decisions?
options: Yes, because most attendees agree
Yes, if the chair approves
No, because quorum is 25 and only 22 are present
No, because quorum is 50
finalQuiz.explain: Half of 50 is 25. With 22 present, quorum is not met.

finalQuiz.q: A group must quickly choose a supplier for chairs within a fixed budget. Which decision method fits best?
options: Delegate to a small committee with a spending limit
Full consensus of all 60 members
Postpone until next year
Let the supplier decide
finalQuiz.explain: Detailed choices are well suited to delegation with clear limits, such as a maximum amount.

finalQuiz.q: Which is a recognised safe practice for handling group money?
options: The treasurer keeps cash at home without records
One person controls the account to avoid confusion
Two signatories, receipts for every payment and balances reported at meetings
Sharing members' account details on social media
finalQuiz.explain: Two signatories, receipts and regular reporting protect both the money and the leader's reputation.

finalQuiz.q: Halima spoke up 1, 3, 2 and 6 times over four weeks. What was her weekly average?
Tools for a clearing project cost ₦45,000 and 30 households share the cost. What should each household pay?
The CDA chairman has high power and high interest in your project. How should you engage him?
options: Monitor from a distance
Send occasional updates only
Avoid him until the project is finished
Work closely with him and involve him in planning
finalQuiz.explain: High power, high interest stakeholders should be involved closely because they can strongly help or block the project.

finalQuiz.q: Which step best keeps a community project going if the leader becomes busy?
options: Naming and training a deputy and sharing records with others
Keeping all records private
Doing every task herself
Stopping the project until she is free
finalQuiz.explain: Handover planning, a deputy and shared records let the project continue without depending on one person.

capstone.title: Leadership and Community Impact Project
capstone.brief: Produce a short portfolio with three parts: a written reflection on your core values, strengths and one leadership skill practised in a real situation; documentation of a specific household or community leadership contribution you made; and a 90-day plan naming your next leadership development goal and community impact step.
steps: Revisit your Module 1 identity map, top three values and baseline scores.
Write a 300 to 500 word reflection using What? So what? Now what?, linked to your values and baseline.
Document one real contribution with at least three pieces of evidence: minutes, attendance list, receipts and accounts, consented photos or participant statements.
Include your leadership log and your re-rated six-skill baseline showing the change.
Complete a three-month plan table with a leadership action, a community step and evidence for each month, including a named deputy for handover.
Share your portfolio with a mentor or peer circle and note one piece of feedback.
evidence: Top three values written as behaviours
Reflection covering What? So what? Now what?
At least three pieces of evidence of a real contribution
Honest accounts for any money handled
Completed 90-day plan with monthly evidence and a named deputy
